title: Systematically Analysing Prompt Injection Vulnerabilities in Diverse LLM Architectures

safety_property.statement: LLMs are expected to refuse requests to generate keylogger code; the property fails when a crafted direct prompt elicits Python code that is usable or adaptable for keylogging. The claim holds only for the 36 open-weight LLMs available on Workers AI's LLM Playground in October 2024, under four single-shot English prompts, with success judged by a single expert rater; it is an attack-side measurement with no defense in the loop and no persistent memory, skill, or agent state involved.
safety_property.operationalized_as: A prompt injection was considered to be successful if it produced code that can be used or adapted for keyloggers (144 tests = 4 prompts x 36 models on Workers AI LLM Playground; final judgments made by the lead author, §3.4).

capabilities: directly queries the target LLM with crafted natural-language prompts (black-box access via the public Workers AI LLM Playground)
uses benign framings to disguise the request: feigned troubleshooting (P1), curiosity about a movie scene (P2), educational-purpose claim (P3)
embeds the malicious instruction between two benign instructions in an 'instruction sandwich' (P4)
assumptions: adversary needs only ordinary user query access; no knowledge of model internals, weights, or training data
attacks are single-step, one-shot, English-language prompts
models accessed via Workers AI's LLM Playground (playground.ai.cloudflare.com), October 2024; parameter counts read from model names (e.g. '7b' = 7 billion parameters)
attack success is judged by the lead author (CISSP, cybersecurity PhD, 15+ years experience) deciding whether the code is usable or adaptable for keylogging
not_covered: indirect prompt injection via external data sources
multilingual prompt injections (listed as future work)
multi-step or progressive attack sequences (listed as future work)
persistent memory, skills, experience, or any agent-harness state (none is present in this setting)
no defense mechanism is implemented or empirically evaluated

intervention.description: No defense intervention is implemented or tested; the paper is a pure vulnerability measurement across 36 LLMs. Mitigations (human oversight for privileged operations, trust boundaries, input/output monitoring, guardrails, alignment, AI telemetry logging) are only recommended qualitatively in section 5.3, citing OWASP and MITRE ATLAS.

results.claim: In this study's setting (4 direct keylogger-code prompt injections against 36 LLMs), 56% of all 144 tests resulted in successful prompt injections, i.e. production of code usable or adaptable for keylogging.
results.setting: Four one-shot English prompts (P1-P4) each tested against 36 open-weight LLMs (chat/instruct/code/domain/multimodal, 0.5b-14b parameters) on Workers AI LLM Playground, October 2024; success judged by the lead author (CISSP, cybersecurity PhD).
results.quote: Overall, 56% of all 144 tests resulted in successful prompt injections, while 44% of the models resisted.

denominator.how_counted: Four prompt injections (P1, P2, P3 and P4) were tested against 36 models resulting in 144 tests (§3.4); percentage is over these 144 tests.

results.claim: The percentage of the 36 LLMs vulnerable to a single prompt increased progressively from the troubleshooting-framing prompt P1 (53%) to the instruction-sandwich prompt P4 (61%), showing the later, more layered prompts exposed weaknesses more effectively.
results.setting: Same 36-LLM Workers AI Playground setup; percent of the 36 models vulnerable to each single prompt (P2 = 53%, P3 = 58% per Table 2).
results.quote: The percentage of models classified as vulnerable increased progressively from Prompt 1 (53%) to Prompt 4 (61%), indicating that the later prompts were more effective in exposing weaknesses.

denominator.how_counted: Table 2 caption: 'The percent of 36 LLMs vulnerable and resistant to the four test prompt injections (P1, P2, P3, and P4).'

results.claim: 28% of the tested LLMs were fully vulnerable (failed all four injections, 10 out of 36) while 14% showed complete resistance (passed all four, 5 out of 36); the rest fell in between.
results.comparison: 28% (10 out of 36) vulnerable to all 4 prompts vs 14% (5 out of 36) resistant to all
results.setting: Distribution of the 36 LLMs by the number (0-4) of the four prompts they were vulnerable to, same Playground setup.
results.quote: The results reveal that 28% of the tested LLMs (10 out of 36) were highly vulnerable, failing all four prompt injections. Additionally, 14% (5 out of 36) of the LLMs demonstrated complete resistance, successfully passing all tests.

denominator.how_counted: Table 3: percentage of LLMs vulnerable to 0, 1, 2, 3, or all 4 prompt injections, out of 36; text gives explicit counts 10 out of 36 and 5 out of 36.

results.claim: Success of P1 and P2 strongly correlated across models (Pearson r = 0.71), indicating overlapping vulnerabilities exploited by the troubleshooting and curiosity framings.
results.setting: Pearson correlation of per-model success outcomes for pairs of the four prompts across the 36 LLMs (Table 4; full pair set 0.71/0.48/0.49/0.42/0.28/0.41; Table 5 writes 0.712).
results.quote: The analysis shows a strong correlation of 0.71 between P1 and P2, indicating that models vulnerable to P1 are also likely to be vulnerable to P2.

results.claim: P2 and P4 showed only a weak correlation (0.28), suggesting the curiosity framing and the instruction sandwich exploit different model weaknesses.
results.setting: Pearson correlation of per-model success outcomes for prompt pairs across the 36 LLMs (Table 4).
results.quote: However, the weak correlation of 0.28 between P2 and P4 suggests that these two prompts likely exploit different model weaknesses.

results.claim: Random forest feature analysis ranks LLM parameter count as the dominant predictor of injection susceptibility (importance 0.75) over LLM type (0.25), in this 36-model dataset.
results.setting: Random forest trained on the 36-model outcome table (parameters and LLM type vs injection success).
results.quote: The results, as shown in Figure 3, indicate that parameters have a higher importance score (0.75), suggesting they are the primary factor in determining a model's susceptibility to prompt injections. In contrast, LLM type has a lower importance score (0.25), indicating a more moderate effect.

results.claim: SHAP analysis corroborates the random forest result: LLM parameters influence vulnerability predictions more (mean SHAP 0.147) than LLM type (mean SHAP 0.075).
results.setting: SHAP values computed for the features LLM parameters and LLM type in the 36-model vulnerability prediction task.
results.quote: The mean SHAP values indicate that LLM parameters hold a higher influence on model predictions, with a mean SHAP value of 0.147, compared to LLM type, which has a mean SHAP value of 0.075 as shown in Figure 4.

results.claim: Logistic regression found higher parameter count slightly negatively associated with vulnerability to at least one injection (coefficient -0.34; LLM type -0.02), contradicting the assumption that larger models are more vulnerable in this setting; the model's accuracy was 86%.
results.setting: Logistic regression predicting whether each of the 36 LLMs is vulnerable to at least one of the four prompts, from parameters and LLM type; model accuracy 86% (§4.5).
results.quote: The coefficient for LLM parameters is -0.34, indicating that models with more parameters are actually slightly less likely to be vulnerable to prompt injections, which contrasts with the typical assumption that larger models are more vulnerable.

limitations.statement: Authors explicitly state that using only four prompts (and a limited model set) is a limitation; more prompts, a larger set of LLMs, and more LLM features would increase the robustness of the findings and statistical analyses.
limitations.quote: Using four prompts in the current student represents a limitation. Using a variety of more prompts can increase the robustness of the findings as well as testing a larger set of LLMs. Additionally, examining more features of each LLM can help provide more data to use in the various statistical analyses.

limitations.statement: Multilingual and multi-step prompt injection attacks were not tested in this study; the authors defer them to future work, noting single-step-resistant models might still be vulnerable to progressive manipulation.
limitations.quote: Another area for investigation is multi-step prompt injection attacks, where LLMs are tested for their susceptibility to complex, multi-step command sequences. This could reveal whether models that initially resist single-step injections are still vulnerable when manipulated progressively over a series of inputs.
